title: How Do the CASEL 5 Relate to the Five Key Beliefs?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by a district PD assignment, Stuart directly compares his own Five Key Beliefs motivation framework to CASEL's widely used SEL framework and concludes they are not, in fact, closely related despite superficial overlap. He characterizes CASEL's Wheel as a description of social-emotional competencies integral to a flourishing life - "a visualization of SEL standards" - while describing his own pyramid as "an x-ray of the human will," a methodology aimed specifically at understanding and cultivating student motivation. He argues the two frameworks can coexist productively: a school already using CASEL could layer the Five Key Beliefs approach on top to help students actually care about becoming competent in CASEL's five areas. He closes with a caution that schools leaning heavily on CASEL should not lose sight of the distinct role of school in a student's life.
points: Draws a clean conceptual line between the two frameworks: CASEL describes social-emotional competencies (an SEL standards visualization) while the Five Key Beliefs diagnoses the mechanics of student motivation (an "x-ray of the human will").

Argues the frameworks are compatible rather than competing - a CASEL-focused school could use the Five Key Beliefs methodology to help students actually care about developing CASEL's five competencies.
Offers a memorable one-line caution for SEL-heavy schools: school shouldn't be Mr. Rogers, it should be "Mr. Rogers in Reverse."
Models transparent framework-building by openly noting the Five Key Beliefs pyramid is his own invention, not an externally validated standard like CASEL's.
quotes: The Five Key Beliefs is a way of understanding how student motivation works and how to help each student grow increasingly motivated to do the work of learning.
CASEL's framework, on the other hand, is describing social-emotional competencies that are integral to the flourishing life.
The CASEL Wheel (and its corresponding explanatory language) is like a visualization of SEL standards. The Five Key Beliefs pyramid, on the other hand, is like an x-ray of the human will.
All that we're doing with 5KB is trying to understand how student motivation works and what role we play as educators in cultivating that motivation.
If a school was interested in CASEL's Wheel, they could apply the 5KB methodology to help more students actually care about growing competent in CASEL's five areas.

I do think that schools emphasizing the CASEL 5 need to be careful not to lose sight of the special role that they play in a student's life. School shouldn't be Mr. Rogers; it should be Mr. Rogers in Reverse.
